Coefficient of Variation (Sample Value or Nearly Unbiased Estimate)

Source: R/cv.R
cv.Rd

Computes the sample coefficient of variation \(k = s / M\), the sample standard deviation divided by the sample mean, or, optionally, the nearly unbiased estimate of Kelley (2007, Equation 4) under normality. Either supply a precomputed cv or supply the raw mean and sd; with unbiased = TRUE the value is multiplied by \((1 + 1/(4 N))\). The (biased) sample coefficient of variation (the default, unbiased = FALSE) is the form usually reported. To accompany it with a confidence interval, use ci_cv.

Usage

cv(cv = NULL, mean = NULL, sd = NULL, N = NULL, unbiased = FALSE)

Arguments

cv

The sample coefficient of variation, \(k = s / M\), a single finite number. Optional; if supplied, mean and sd must not be.

mean

Sample mean. A single finite number other than 0. A negative mean gives a negative coefficient; ci_cv requires a positive one.

sd

Sample standard deviation, using \(N - 1\) in the variance denominator. A single finite number that is not negative.

N

Sample size. Required when unbiased = TRUE, where it must exceed 1.

unbiased

Logical. If TRUE, multiplies the sample value by \((1 + 1/(4 N))\). The result is nearly, not exactly, unbiased (see Details). Default FALSE.

Value

A 1-row data.frame with columns term and value. The term value is "cv" and value is either the sample coefficient (default) or the nearly unbiased estimate (when unbiased = TRUE).

Details

The sample coefficient of variation \(k = s / M\) is the form usually reported in applied work. It is what this function returns by default (unbiased = FALSE). A point estimate is most informative when paired with a confidence interval; ci_cv computes one for the population value \(\kappa\).

Under normality the sample coefficient is biased. Its expected value is approximately \(\kappa [1 - 1/(4 (N - 1)) + \kappa^2/N]\), the first and second order terms of Expression 3 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 51), which Kelley (2007) reproduces as his Equation 3. The term \(-1/(4 (N - 1))\) comes from the sample standard deviation and the term \(\kappa^2/N\) from the sample mean in the denominator, so \(k\) underestimates \(\kappa\) on average when \(\kappa\) is below about one half and overestimates it when \(\kappa\) is larger. Multiplying \(k\) by \((1 + 1/(4 N))\), a correction that Sokal and Braumann (1980) and Kelley (2007) credit to Haldane (1955), offsets the first term and not the second. The relative bias that remains is about \(\kappa^2/N - 9/(32 N^2)\); the second of these terms is derived from the expected value of \(s\) under normality and is not taken from those sources. Kelley (2007, Equation 4) calls the result a nearly unbiased estimate and recommends it when a point estimate is reported; the sample value \(k\) is the one used to form the confidence interval.

At \(\kappa = 0.1\) and \(N = 10\) the relative bias is about \(-2.6\) percent for \(k\) and \(-0.2\) percent for the corrected value; at \(\kappa = 0.3\) and \(N = 10\) it is about \(-1.8\) percent and \(+0.6\) percent. With 10 cases the two are about equally biased, in opposite directions, at a coefficient near 0.38 (near 0.35 in large samples, and above 0.4 with 5 cases or fewer), and for a larger \(\kappa\) the corrected value is the more biased of the two. These statements describe a mean that stays away from 0: under an unrestricted normal distribution the expectation of \(1/M\) does not exist as an ordinary integral.

For confidence intervals on \(\kappa\), ci_cv inverts the noncentral t distribution of \(\sqrt{N}/k\) (Johnson & Welch, 1940; McKay, 1932; Kelley, 2007). McKay (1932) and Vangel (1996) also give approximations based on the chi square distribution, which ci_cv does not use. The first-order variance of \(k\) under normality, \(\kappa^2 (1/2 + \kappa^2) / (N - 1)\), is in var_cv, whose page relates it to Expression 5 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 52).

References

Haldane, J. B. S. (1955). The measurement of variation. Evolution, 9(4), 484. doi:10.1111/j.1558-5646.1955.tb01559.x

Johnson, N. L., & Welch, B. L. (1940). Applications of the non-central t-distribution. Biometrika, 31(3–4), 362–389. doi:10.1093/biomet/31.3-4.362

Kelley, K. (2007). Sample size planning for the coefficient of variation from the accuracy in parameter estimation approach. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 755–766. doi:10.3758/BF03192966

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

McKay, A. T. (1932). Distribution of the coefficient of variation and the extended t distribution. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 95(4), 695–698.

Sokal, R. R., & Braumann, C. A. (1980). Significance tests for coefficients of variation and variability profiles. Systematic Zoology, 29(1), 50–66. doi:10.1093/sysbio/29.1.50

Vangel, M. G. (1996). Confidence intervals for a normal coefficient of variation. The American Statistician, 50(1), 21–26. doi:10.1080/00031305.1996.10473537

See also

ci_cv, var_cv, ss_aipe_cv

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# 1. Point estimate from raw mean and SD.
cv(mean = 100, sd = 15)
#>  term value
#>  cv   0.150

# 2. Nearly unbiased estimate at N = 50; the multiplier is close to 1
#    at this sample size.
cv(mean = 100, sd = 15, N = 50, unbiased = TRUE)
#>  term value
#>  cv   0.151

# 3. The same at N = 10, where the multiplier is larger.
cv(cv = .15, N = 10, unbiased = TRUE)
#>  term value
#>  cv   0.154
